title: Five hundred years together (2016)
hookLine: Lutherans and Catholics mark the Reformation's anniversary by praying together in Lund

lines: A POPE AND LUTHERAN LEADERS, TOGETHER.
cards: A Lutheran cathedral in Lund, a city in the south of Sweden. At the front stand the pope, dressed in white, and the leaders of the Lutheran World Federation.

They're there to mark an anniversary: the Reformation, the break that sent Catholics and Lutherans down separate roads, often against each other, sometimes in blood. A strange thing to commemorate together.
And yet they've come to pray, in one service, from one book.

teach.h: A DOOR IN WITTENBERG, AND A LONG DIVISION.
teach.b: Tradition says the Reformation began when a monk named Martin Luther posted his arguments on a church door in Wittenberg.
What followed was division, and much worse: wars, burnings and generations of suspicion on both sides. Past anniversaries had been kept apart, by one side without the other. Lund was different.
Before it, Catholic and Lutheran theologians had worked through their history together and published a report whose title became today's line: From Conflict to Communion.
They had already agreed on a joint statement on justification, how a person is made right with God, the very question Luther had fought over. So the service at Lund did three things.
It gave thanks for gifts each side had received through the Reformation. It confessed, out loud, the harm each side had done to the other.
And it made promises: to keep praying together, to work together for the poor, to seek full unity.

The pope and the Lutheran leaders signed a joint statement there, with one honest note: Catholics and Lutherans still don't share communion at one table, and the statement named that as a pain they long to heal.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: Behind it all stands a prayer of Jesus in John's Gospel, on the night before he died, in the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us."
Paul has his own picture: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." Lund didn't end the division. It turned the two sides around to face each other.

how: Catholics and Lutherans hold joint services of prayer in some places, using a common order of worship prepared for the Reformation commemoration, with thanksgiving, confession and commitment to unity.

practice: Think of a Christian of a different kind than the one you know best, or, if you aren't a Christian, someone whose faith you don't share, and picture their face.
Name one gift you've received through them or their tradition, then one thing you might owe them an apology for, or simply one assumption you've made.
If you pray, pray Jesus's line from John, that they all may be one; if not, simply wish them well.
